ISRO problem statement · urban heat

Finding the hottest blocks in 50 Indian cities, from space

A U-Net reads Landsat and land-cover layers and predicts which parts of a city run hotter or cooler than the city's own average (late-morning pass, March to May). It learned from 40 cities and was scored on 10 held out from training.

01 · Overview

Which parts of a city are cooking, why, and how much green would it take to cool them down?

The problem, objective and motivation, as the project README states them.

Problem

Heat is not spread evenly inside a city. The README asks which parts of a city are cooking, what drives that heat, and how much change would cool those places down.

Objective

Build a satellite dataset of 50 Indian cities, train a U-Net to predict how heat is spread inside a city, and turn it into three tools: a hotspot finder, a "what is driving this heat?" explainer and a cooling what-if simulator.

Why it matters

Three tools

1. Where are the hotspots?

The model predicts every pixel's temperature, and Getis-Ord Gi* flags blocks that are significantly hotter than the rest of the city. There is no "top 10 %" quota. models/hotspot_report.py

2. What is driving them?

Features are grouped (vegetation, built-up, albedo, water, terrain, land cover). Swapping one group at a time for the neighbours' average gives each group's share of the extra heat, in °C (Shapley values). models/hotspot_report.py

3. What would cool it down?

The simulator converts a growing share of an area to tree cover and/or reflective roofs, re-predicts, and reports the dose at which the area is as cool as its surroundings. models/simulate_cooling.py

Source: README.md L3-52 (tagline, 30-second version, three tools); numbers from cooling.json rows[1].

02 · Methodology

From satellite scenes to a per-pixel temperature-anomaly model

Each city is a 40 km square on a 30 m grid. The model predicts where a city's ground is hotter or cooler than that city's own average. The temperature is land surface temperature (how hot ground and roofs are, measured from space), not air temperature.

Pipeline

    Source: 03_methodology.md §2 (stages and scripts checked against the code at HEAD 6e20bf7).

    Data sources

    SourceWhat it providesResolutionPeriodAccess
    Landsat 8/9 Collection 2 Level-2 (landsat-c2-l2)Thermal band → LST (the target). Six reflectance bands → NDVI, NDBI, MNDWI, albedo. QA band → cloud mask30 m gridMar-May, 2022-2025; up to 40 clearest scenes per cityMicrosoft Planetary Computer STAC
    Copernicus DEM GLO-30 (cop-dem-glo-30)Elevation, from which slope is computed30 mstaticPlanetary Computer
    ESA WorldCover (esa-worldcover)Land-cover class (11 codes, 80 = water)10 m product, resampled to 30 m by majority2021Planetary Computer
    JRC GHSL R2023ABuilding height (2018), built-up surface (2020), population (2020)3 arcsec (~90 m), resampled to 30 m2018 / 2020Direct download from the JRC FTP server
    Open-Meteo archive (ERA5-based)Air temperature, humidity, wind, sunlight and rain around the overpass hoursone value per cityscene datesPublic API, no key
    OpenStreetMap (optional --osm)Building, water and green fractions30 mcurrentosmnx

    Weather and OSM are not model inputs. The Open-Meteo values are stored as city-level constants in the audit tables and never reach the U-Net. Google Earth Engine is not used.

    Source: 03_methodology.md §3 (extraction/build_dataset.py; README.md L248-250).

    Model

    All 51 input channel names (from the checkpoint)

    Inputs: 46 features per pixel plus 6 city-relative copies

    • Surface (4): NDVI, NDBI, MNDWI, albedo.
    • Terrain (2): elevation, slope. Land cover (1): WorldCover class, learned as a 4-number code.
    • Urban form (3): GHSL building height, built-up fraction, population.
    • Distances (2): to water and to green, in metres.
    • Neighbourhood means (6) over 150 m and 450 m, and surroundings (28): window means from 90 m to 2,010 m plus local variation.
    • City-relative copies (6): NDVI, NDBI, albedo, built-up, height and elevation, re-expressed against the city's own mean and spread.

    Training

    • Huber loss on standardised anomalies, usable pixels only; AdamW (lr 2e-3, weight decay 1e-2), one-cycle schedule, batch 64.
    • Random 90° rotations and flips, dropout 0.1, weight averaging (EMA 0.998). Final run --base 32 --epochs 7 on a 4-core CPU.
    • Cities split whole: 40 for training, 10 held out from training (also used to pick the best epoch): .

    Source: 03_methodology.md §4-5 (models/train_unet.py; pre_processing/make_patches.py).

    Evaluation

    Scores are per held-out city, on usable pixels. The city's true mean is added back before scoring, so the scores measure the pattern inside the city. Three models were compared on the same pixels; there is no non-neural baseline and no ablation.

    MetricPlain meaningWhat "good" looks likeFinal model, mean of the 10 held-out cities
    • Validation caveat. The 10 held-out cities never trained the weights, but they picked the best epoch and ranked the models, so the scores are slightly optimistic. The README says to think "about 0.7". One split, one run, no confidence intervals.
    • Other checks: Gi* hotspot-cluster overlap for Delhi and Jaipur, a vegetation sanity check against the satellite data, and group permutation importance. All three appear under Results.

    How the tool finds hotspots, explains them and simulates cooling

    Hotspots (Getis-Ord Gi*)

    Predicted temperature is averaged into 600 m blocks (300 m in live mode). Gi* over each 3 × 3 block neighbourhood flags blocks with z ≥ 2.58. Touching blocks join into clusters of 2+ blocks, kept only if at least 1 °C above a 900 m ring of neighbours.

    Drivers (Shapley values)

    Six feature groups. For all 26 = 64 combinations, groups switched "off" take the neighbour ring's values and the model predicts again. Each group gets its exact Shapley share in °C. These are the model's attributions, not proven causes.

    Cooling doses

    Vegetation converts non-water pixels with NDVI < 0.4 to the city's median tree values; cool roofs raise built pixels' albedo by 0.15 (cap 0.6). After each step the features are recomputed and the model re-predicts. The dose is the share converted when the area matches its ring.

    Source: 03_methodology.md §7 (models/hotspot_report.py, models/simulate_cooling.py, dashboard/app.py).

              04 · Infrastructure

              Where the pipeline ran, and how the app ships

              Only what the repository supports. The compute instance is inferred from the README and scripts; the repo has no job definitions or workspace config.

              Compute and data

              • Azure ML compute instance (inferred). The README says the project was "developed on a 4-core Azure ML instance" with about 32 GB RAM; extraction/run_new_cities.sh falls back to the azureml_py38 conda env; Deploy/README.md names paths "on the Azure VM". Training ran on CPU.
              • Results are files on the compute instance's disk (data/, pre_processing/), gitignored. Only Deploy/best.pt is committed.
              • No Azure Storage is used in code: no storage account, blob container, abfs:// or wasb:// path, connection string or Azure SDK. The only SAS tokens are Planetary Computer's own short-lived public signing tokens.
              • Inputs are public: Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC (Landsat, DEM, WorldCover) and the JRC GHSL server.

              Build and deploy

              • GitHub Actions CI on every push and PR: syntax check, then unit and app tests on a synthetic 200 × 200 px city with an untrained model (no real data, no network).
              • GHCR: on main, the image job checks for Deploy/best.pt and Deploy/meta.json, then pushes ghcr.io/<repo>:latest and :<sha>. Deploy/meta.json is missing today, so this job would fail.
              • Optional deploy via repo variable DEPLOY_TARGET: azure (OIDC login, az containerapp update; README setup: heat-rg, centralindia, app urban-heat, 2 CPU / 4 GiB) or huggingface (Docker Space).
              • Docker: python:3.12-slim, CPU PyTorch 2.5.1, Streamlit on port 8501 with a health check; about 4 GB RAM and internet access for live mode.

              Source: 03_methodology.md §8; 02_data_inventory.md (a); 01_project_brief.md §8-9 (Dockerfile, .github/workflows/ci.yml, README.md L91-105, L263).

              05 · Limitations & next steps

              What the numbers do not show

                Author notes: next steps and open questions

                Next steps

                • Copy the raw outputs off the compute instance. Priority 1 is a few MB of CSVs (eval_per_city.csv, model_comparison*.csv, group_importance.csv, *_hotspots.csv, sim_*.csv) plus pre_processing/patches/meta.json. data/build_data.py picks them up automatically.
                • Replace the placeholder heat map with a downsampled predicted grid (*_pred.npy minus its mean) for a held-out city. The renderer switches off every placeholder label when _placeholder is false.
                • Add Deploy/meta.json from the same run as best.pt, so CI's image job and the Streamlit app can run.
                • Report uncertainty: a second split or seed, or leave-one-city-out, would give the scores a spread.

                Open questions for the author

                1. The README headline "R² 0.74 inside the city" is the offset-removed mean; the as-scored mean is 0.72. Which should the dashboard lead with?
                2. Can we describe the 10 validation cities as "held out from training, used for model selection" everywhere, including the README hero table?
                3. Were the README cooling doses and fig_cooling_curves.png produced with the final model (data/unet_run3)? simulate_cooling.py defaults to unet_run2. Is Deploy/best.pt that same checkpoint?
                4. Which definition should the dashboard call a "hotspot": Gi* clusters (the tool) or the hottest 10 % of pixels (behind the AUC and F1)?
                5. Is the "about 2.4 °C not explained" for the Delhi block computed from unrounded values? The table's rounded values give 2.5 °C.
                6. Can you share the raw evaluation CSVs, including RMSE, skill and IoU, which are computed but not reported?
                7. Which cities were judged "hardest" and kept in training, and were multiple seeds or splits ever tried?

                Source: 03_methodology.md §9-10; 04_insights.md §6; insights.json inconsistencies.
